title: Count Palindromic Substrings

concept.title: Every successful expansion is one palindrome
body: Expanding around a centre finds a whole family of palindromes: when the letters at `l` and `r` match, the block `s[l..r]` is a palindrome, and expanding once more may give the next one. So **each step of the expansion that succeeds is one more palindromic substring**.

body.code:
count = 0
for c in range(2 * n - 1):
    l = c // 2
    r = l + c % 2
    while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
        count += 1        # s[l..r] is a palindrome
        l -= 1
        r += 1

body: Substrings are counted by their position, so equal substrings at different places count separately. In `aaa` there are 6: three `a`, two `aa` and one `aaa`.

statement: Count the palindromic substrings of a word. Substrings at different positions are counted separately, even if they consist of the same letters.
inputFormat: A single word of lowercase letters.
outputFormat: Print the number of palindromic substrings.

examples.note: a, a, a, aa, aa, aaa: six substrings.

hints: Use the same centres as for the longest palindrome.
Every time the two outer letters match during an expansion, you found one more palindrome.
Add one to the counter at each successful step.

explanation: Each successful expansion step around a centre corresponds to exactly one palindromic substring.

code.python:
s = input().strip()

n = len(s)
count = 0
for c in range(2 * n - 1):
    l = c // 2
    rr = l + c % 2
    while l >= 0 and rr < n and s[l] == s[rr]:
        count += 1
        l -= 1
        rr += 1
print(count)
